body.text: Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro yesterday wrapped up a two-day humanitarian mission in Myanmar, potentially her last as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s special envoy to the country.

According to the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Lazaro began her mission with a visit to the city of Taunggyi in a military-controlled region of Shan State, to oversee the distribution of aid through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance.

She then traveled yesterday to the capital Naypyidaw, where she met with Myanmar’s Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe. The two officials discussed “the humanitarian situation and hard-to-reach communities, as well as the overall implementation of the Five-Point Consensus,” ASEAN’s plan for managing the Myanmar conflict, the DFA said in a statement.

While in Naypyidaw, Lazaro also visited a school and monastery in Pyinmana Township that were granted Philippine humanitarian assistance after the devastating earthquake of March 2025. The DFA added that she concluded her mission in Yangon, where she held “consultations with ASEAN Embassies.”

Unsurprisingly, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry characterized yesterday’s meeting between Lazaro and Tin Maung Swe differently, stating that the two envoys “held substantive discussions on ways to restore Myanmar’s original role and rights within ASEAN.” The Myanmar foreign minister informed Lazaro of the government’s efforts to promote peace and stability, address “terrorism,” and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and “underscored Myanmar’s full cooperation under the ASEAN framework.”

The Five-Point Consensus, promulgated by ASEAN two months after the military coup, calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to Myanmar’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid. However, the military’s failure to implement the most important terms of the Consensus prompted ASEAN to exclude Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings in late 2021.

Since taking office in April, the new military-backed administration headed by coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard for normalization with ASEAN. Five ASEAN member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.

At the same time, it has explicitly rejected the Five-Point Consensus and denounced ASEAN for its “discrimination.” While the Myanmar Foreign Ministry stated that Tin Maung Swe “highlighted the Government’s constructive cooperation towards implementing the ASEAN Five-Point Statement” – it now refuses to refer to it as a “Consensus” – he added that it would do so “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives,” some of which directly contradict the ASEAN plan.

It is thus unsurprising that Naypyidaw would seek to characterize Lazaro’s visit as a step on the road toward the current Myanmar regime’s relegitimization. Indeed, as one observer noted today on X, allowing Lazaro to preside over the distribution of humanitarian aid in Taunggyi, far from most of the active conflict zones in Shan State, allows the Philippines to claim progress on the Five-Point Consensus.

Notably, though perhaps not surprisingly, Lazaro, whose position as special envoy will end when Singapore takes over ASEAN’s chairmanship in 2027, concluded her mission without meeting detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

The 81-year-old has been in custody since the coup, but the military-backed government has loosened the terms of her detention somewhat over the last six months, in pursuit of its goal of regional normalization. After announcing her move from prison to house arrest in April, it has released photos of her meeting with a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross. This month, it also allowed her to receive two books and a diplomatic package from Britain’s King Charles III and to hold a phone call with her son, Kim Aris.

As ASEAN chair in 2026, the Philippines has pressed Naypyidaw for access to the Nobel laureate. It made its first request for “brief access” after she was moved to house arrest in April and again in August after she was allowed to meet with the ICRC representative. The Myanmar administration refused both.

While Myanmar is keen to use Aung San Suu Kyi to extract concessions from its key partners, it is clear that this will stop short of recognizing her as a legitimate political interlocutor. Moreover, having rejected the need for an ASEAN special envoy at all back in August, the outcome of Lazaro’s mission is a sign that Naypyidaw will use ASEAN’s special envoys not to advance the Five-Point Consensus, but to support its chosen pursuit of political consolidation at home and diplomatic normalization abroad.
